title: Option Strategies
intro: Combining options with each other and with the stock gives payoffs of almost any shape. A few combinations cover nearly everything individual investors do: generating income from shares, insuring them, betting on a direction with limited risk, and betting on how much a price will move rather than which way. Use the plot to see each one at expiry and today.

widget.title: Option strategy profit (stock bought at 100; strikes around 100)

blocks.text: Premiums in the plot come from the Black-Scholes model at the volatility you set, with the stock at 100 when the position is opened. The 'today' curve shows what the position would be worth if the stock jumped there immediately, so the gap between it and the expiry curve is the time value still in the options.
Income: covered calls and cash-secured puts

A covered call holds 100 shares and sells one call above the current price (in the plot, strike 110). You keep the premium, and if the stock rises past the strike your shares are called away at the strike: you have swapped the upside beyond 110 for cash now. The downside is almost the same as owning the stock, cushioned only by the premium. Covered calls do well in flat or gently rising markets and lag in strong rallies. Buy-write indexes such as the CBOE BXM have historically delivered somewhat lower returns than the S&P 500 with lower volatility.

A cash-secured put sells a put and sets aside the cash to buy the shares if assigned. By put-call parity, a short put is economically almost the same as a covered call at the same strike: both collect premium and both lose if the stock falls a lot. Selling puts is a way to be paid while waiting to buy a stock at a lower price.

A protective put owns the stock and buys a put below the price (strike 90 in the plot). Below 90 your loss is frozen; above it you keep the upside, minus the premium. Insurance has a cost: buying puts continuously has been expensive over time, because implied volatility usually exceeds the volatility that later occurs.

A collar owns the stock, buys a put below and sells a call above. The call premium pays for much or all of the put (a 'zero-cost collar'), at the price of capping the upside. Executives with concentrated stock positions often use collars.
Directional bets with limited risk: vertical spreads

A bull call spread buys a call at one strike and sells a call at a higher strike (100 and 115 in the plot). The sold call lowers the cost, and caps the gain at the difference between strikes minus the net premium. A bear put spread is the mirror image for a fall. Spreads cost less than a single option and lose less when volatility falls, but give up the big payoff.
Volatility bets: straddles, strangles and condors

items: Long straddle: buy a call and a put at the same strike. It profits if the stock moves a lot in either direction, more than the two premiums combined; it loses if the stock stays still. Traders buy straddles before events like earnings when they think the market underprices the coming move.
Long strangle: the same with an OTM call and an OTM put; cheaper, needs a bigger move.
Short straddle and strangle: sell them, collecting premium and betting on calm. Profits are limited and losses can be very large.
Iron condor: sell an OTM put and an OTM call, and buy further-out ones to cap the loss. A defined-risk bet that the stock stays in a range (in the plot, between about 90 and 110).
Butterfly: buy one call at a low strike, sell two in the middle, buy one at a high strike; pays most if the stock ends exactly at the middle strike.
Calendar spread: sell a near-dated option and buy a later one at the same strike, profiting from the faster time decay of the near option.

blocks.text: The expected move the market prices in is roughly the cost of the at-the-money straddle: for a stock at 100 with an ATM straddle at 8, the market expects a move of about 8% by expiry. A useful approximation for that straddle is $0.8\,\sigma\sqrt{T}\,S$.

items: Assignment: American options can be exercised early; short calls are most often assigned the day before an ex-dividend date when the dividend exceeds the remaining time value.
Liquidity: use options with tight bid-ask spreads and real open interest; on thinly traded options the spread alone can eat the expected edge.
Position size: limit the total premium at risk; a spread's 'max loss' is a real number you will sometimes hit.
Brokers require approval levels: covered calls and protective puts first; naked short options last.

blocks.title: Covered call outcome
blocks.text: You own 100 shares bought at \$100 and sell a 110-strike call for \$2.50. At expiry the stock is at \$125. What is your profit, and what would it have been without the call?
solution: Shares are called away at \$110: gain $= (110 - 100 + 2.50) \times 100 = \$1{,}250$.
Without the call: $(125 - 100) \times 100 = \$2{,}500$. The call cost you \$1,250 of upside in exchange for the \$250 premium.

blocks.title: Bull call spread
blocks.text: You buy a 100-strike call for \$6 and sell a 110-strike call for \$2.50. What are your maximum gain, maximum loss and break-even?

blocks.title: Straddle before earnings
blocks.text: A stock is at \$80. The 80-strike call costs \$4.10 and the 80-strike put \$3.90, both expiring just after earnings. How far must the stock move for a long straddle to profit? If the stock has typically moved 7% on earnings, is it cheap?
solution: Cost $= \$8.00$, so it needs a move beyond 72 or 88: 10% either way.

A typical 7% move (\$5.60) would leave you with about \$5.60 of value against \$8.00 paid. On this history the straddle looks expensive; selling it (with defined risk, say as an iron condor) would be the side the history favors, with the risk that this time is different.

blocks.title: Collar
blocks.text: You own a stock at \$200. You buy a 180 put for \$5 and sell a 230 call for \$5. What is the range of outcomes at expiry?
solution: Net premium 0. The worst case is selling at \$180 (−\$20, −10%); the best is \$230 (+\$30, +15%). Between, you get the stock's own move.
